questions: Which component collects metrics in the OpenShift built-in monitoring stack?
OpenShift monitoring uses Prometheus for metrics collection and storage, Alertmanager for alerts and Thanos Querier for aggregated queries.
Platform metrics such as node CPU and pod memory are scraped by Prometheus in openshift-monitoring.
Metrics: Prometheus. Logs: Loki or Elasticsearch. Traces: Tempo, Jaeger or Instana.
What must be enabled for Prometheus to scrape metrics from CP4I workloads in user namespaces using the built-in OpenShift monitoring?
Monitoring for user-defined projects (enableUserWorkload: true in the cluster-monitoring-config ConfigMap)
Platform monitoring covers OpenShift components by default. Workload metrics in user namespaces need user workload monitoring enabled. ServiceMonitors or PodMonitors then define the scrape targets.
After enabling user workload monitoring, MQ and ACE metrics appear under Observe > Metrics.
No workload metrics? Check that user workload monitoring is enabled.
What does a ServiceMonitor resource define?
Which Services' endpoints Prometheus should scrape for metrics, including port, path and interval
ServiceMonitors (and PodMonitors) are Prometheus Operator CRs that describe scrape targets declaratively.
A ServiceMonitor selects the queue manager metrics Service on port 9157.
Metrics exposed but not collected -> check the ServiceMonitor selector.
Which observability pillars should an integration monitoring architecture cover?
Metrics, logs and distributed traces, correlated by common identifiers, plus alerting and dashboards
Metrics show trends and thresholds, logs show events and errors, and traces show request paths across components. Correlation ties them together.
A trace ID in ACE logs links to the trace in the APM tool and the API Connect analytics record.
A company runs 5 OpenShift clusters with CP4I. Operations wants a single view of metrics and alerts with long-term retention. Which architecture is MOST appropriate?

Keep per-cluster Prometheus (platform and user workload) and forward or remote-write selected metrics to a central, scalable store (for example Thanos, Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management observability, or an enterprise APM), with centralized alert routing and dashboards
Point all clusters' pods to one Prometheus in cluster 1
Increase local Prometheus retention to 5 years on each cluster
Use only email notifications from each cluster
Federated or remote-write designs give a central view and long retention while each cluster keeps local collection for resilience.
Correct: local collection plus central aggregation.
Wrong: a single point of failure and does not scale.
Wrong: local storage is limited and fragmented.
ACM Observability aggregates metrics from all managed clusters into object storage with 13 months of retention.
Which OpenShift capability collects container logs and forwards them to a log store or external systems?
OpenShift Logging (Vector collector with ClusterLogForwarder, storing in LokiStack or forwarding to external destinations)
OpenShift Logging collects node and container logs and can store them in Loki or forward them to Splunk, Elasticsearch, Kafka or syslog.
ClusterLogForwarder sends cp4i-prod application logs to the enterprise Splunk.
Logs off the node quickly; pods and nodes are ephemeral.
Why should integration logs be centralized rather than read only with oc logs?
Pod logs are lost when pods are deleted or rescheduled, and centralization enables searching, correlation and retention across replicas
Container logs on nodes are ephemeral and scattered. Centralized logging preserves and correlates them.
After a crash and reschedule, the old pod's logs remain searchable in Loki.
Which logging practice BEST supports troubleshooting across ACE, MQ and API Connect?
Structured (JSON) logs including a correlation or transaction ID propagated from the API through the flow and message headers
Logging full payloads of all messages at debug level in production
Structured logs with propagated correlation IDs let one transaction be traced across components and searched efficiently.
Wrong: data protection and volume issues.
An X-Correlation-ID from the gateway is copied into MQ message properties and ACE log entries.
Correlation IDs are the glue of integration observability.
Logs from CP4I pods are missing in the central log store, but other namespaces' logs arrive. What should be checked?
The ClusterLogForwarder pipelines and inputs (namespace selection), collector status on the nodes, and output errors or rate limits
Log forwarding is configured per input and pipeline. Namespace selectors, collector problems or output throttling can drop logs for specific namespaces.
Correct: forwarder configuration and collector health.
The forwarder input only included namespaces matching 'app-*', not 'cp4i-*'.
Missing logs for some namespaces -> inputs and selectors.
Log volume from CP4I in production suddenly increases tenfold, overloading the log store. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
Debug or trace logging was left enabled (for example ACE user trace or verbose logging); return to production log levels and enforce log-level policies through configuration management
The log store is too efficient
Diagnostic logging enabled in production is a common cause of log floods, extra cost and data exposure.
An ACE serverconf with user trace enabled was promoted by mistake; the pipeline now blocks trace settings in production.
Diagnostic levels must be time-boxed and controlled.
How does an MQ queue manager deployed by the CP4I operator expose metrics for Prometheus?
Through a built-in metrics endpoint (enabled in the QueueManager CR) that publishes queue manager and queue statistics in Prometheus format
The MQ container exposes Prometheus metrics (by default on port 9157 when metrics are enabled), derived from MQ resource statistics.
Wrong: not the only way, and not Prometheus.
spec.queueManager.metrics.enabled: true and a ServiceMonitor scrapes qm1's metrics.
MQ metrics endpoint + ServiceMonitor = Prometheus integration.
Which metric is MOST useful for detecting a stopped consumer on an MQ queue?
Queue depth increasing combined with low or zero get rate (or growing oldest-message age)
Rising depth with no gets indicates the consumer is not processing. Oldest-message age is an excellent latency signal.
Correct: depth, get rate and message age.
An alert fires when ORDERS.IN depth is over 1,000 and the get rate is 0 for 5 minutes.
Depth alone can mislead; combine it with rates and age.
Which metric is the PRIMARY indicator that Kafka consumers are falling behind?
Consumer group lag (difference between log-end offset and committed offset per partition)

Consumer lag is the difference between a partition's log-end offset and the group's committed offset. It directly measures how many records are waiting to be processed. Growing lag means consumers are slower than producers. Per-partition lag also reveals hot keys or a single slow consumer.
Lag for group billing on topic orders exceeds 50,000 and triggers an alert.
Watch lag trends, not only absolute values.
Which TWO broker-level metrics indicate a Kafka replication or availability risk? (Select TWO.)
Under-replicated partitions show reduced redundancy; offline partitions show unavailability. Both need alerts.
Kafka producer latency spikes periodically, and broker metrics show request queue time and disk I/O wait rising at the same moments. What is the MOST likely root cause?
Storage I/O saturation on brokers (for example noisy neighbours on shared storage or log segment flushing and compaction), delaying request handling
Consumers using the wrong group ID
Correlated disk wait and request queue time point to storage bottlenecks. Investigate storage performance and isolation.
Moving brokers to dedicated SSD volumes eliminated the spikes.
Correlate latency with resource metrics to find the bottleneck.
An ACE API's response time doubled, but CPU and memory are normal. Which metrics should be examined next?
Flow and node statistics (elapsed time per node) to see which node or external call (for example a database or HTTP request) contributes the most time

ACE accounting and statistics record message counts, CPU and elapsed time per flow and per node. When response time grows but CPU and memory are normal, the runtime is usually waiting on something. Node-level elapsed times show whether an HTTPRequest, Database or MQ node (an external dependency) accounts for the delay.
Statistics showed the HTTPRequest node to the CRM taking 1.8 s of the 2 s total.
Normal CPU plus slow responses means waiting on a dependency.
Which set of 'golden signals' should be monitored for each integration service?
The four golden signals give a balanced view of service health from the user's perspective and of resource limits.
API dashboards show p95 latency, requests per second, 5xx rate and gateway CPU saturation.
An architect defines an SLO of 99.9% successful API calls over 30 days. Which alerting approach is BEST?
Error-budget burn-rate alerts (multi-window, for example fast and slow burn) based on the SLI, rather than alerting on every individual error or a fixed CPU threshold
Alert on every single failed call
Alert only at month-end if the SLO is missed
Burn-rate alerts detect when the error budget is being consumed too fast, which balances fast detection with low noise.
Wrong: not tied to user impact.
Page if the 1-hour burn rate is above 14.4x; open a ticket if the 6-hour burn rate is above 6x.
Alert on user impact (SLO), not on every symptom.
Recording the path and timing of a single request as it flows through multiple services, as spans linked by a trace ID

A distributed trace follows one request across services. Each unit of work is a span with timing and attributes, and spans are linked by a shared trace ID that travels in headers or message properties. The trace shows where time is spent end to end and which dependency failed, which metrics and logs alone cannot show.
One trace shows gateway (20 ms) -> ACE (40 ms) -> MQ put -> back end (300 ms).
A vendor-neutral open standard and set of SDKs and collectors for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs
OpenTelemetry (OTel) standardizes instrumentation and export (OTLP), so telemetry can be sent to many backends.
ACE exports spans by OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector, which forwards them to Instana or Tempo.
How is trace context propagated between an HTTP client and an ACE REST API so spans link into one trace?
Through standard trace context headers (for example W3C traceparent), which the receiving service reads to continue the trace
Context propagation passes the trace ID and parent span ID between services. For messaging, context travels in message headers or properties.
The gateway forwards traceparent; ACE continues the trace and adds it to MQ message properties.
Traces show the API Gateway and ACE spans but break at MQ: the downstream consumer starts a new, unrelated trace. What is the cause?
Trace context is not propagated in the MQ message (for example missing trace properties or the consumer not extracting them), so the consumer cannot link to the parent trace
Asynchronous hops need context carried in message metadata, and consumers must extract it. Otherwise traces fragment.
Correct: missing propagation across the messaging hop.
Enabling OpenTelemetry context propagation in MQ message properties for both producer and consumer linked the traces.
Async hops: put context in message headers or properties.
A company wants end-to-end tracing across API Connect, DataPower, ACE, MQ and Kafka with minimal vendor lock-in. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

Standardize on OpenTelemetry: enable OTel or APM tracing where each product supports it (for example ACE OpenTelemetry), propagate W3C trace context across HTTP and message headers, route spans through an OpenTelemetry Collector to the chosen backend (for example Instana or Tempo), and sample appropriately
Write custom log parsers for each product and stitch them manually
OTel offers a common protocol and collector layer. Propagation across sync and async hops plus sampling gives end-to-end visibility at manageable cost.
Correct: OTel standardization with a collector.
Wrong: data protection and cost issues.
The collector tail-samples 100% of error traces and 5% of successful ones.
What value does an APM tool such as IBM Instana add for CP4I operations?
Automatic discovery of components and dependencies, distributed tracing, and correlation of traces with infrastructure and application metrics for faster root-cause analysis
APM tools build dependency maps and link traces, metrics and events, which shortens mean time to resolution.
Instana highlights that latency spikes in ACE correlate with GC pauses in a downstream Java service.
Spans are generated in ACE but never appear in the tracing backend. What should be checked FIRST?
The exporter configuration (OTLP endpoint, protocol and port), network policies to the collector, and collector logs for rejected data
Telemetry export problems usually come from wrong endpoints, blocked network paths or collector pipeline errors.
A NetworkPolicy blocked egress to the collector on port 4317; allowing it restored traces.
No traces -> check the exporter to collector path.
Which OpenShift component routes alerts to notification channels such as email, Slack or PagerDuty?
Prometheus evaluates rules and fires alerts; Alertmanager groups, deduplicates and routes them to receivers.
Critical MQ alerts route to PagerDuty; warnings go to a Slack channel.
How are custom alert rules for CP4I workloads defined in OpenShift user workload monitoring?
With PrometheusRule resources in the workload namespace containing PromQL expressions, durations and labels

With OpenShift user workload monitoring, alerting and recording rules are declared as PrometheusRule custom resources in the workload's namespace. Each rule has a PromQL expression, a 'for' duration and labels or annotations used for routing and runbook links. Alertmanager then routes the resulting alerts.
A PrometheusRule for a CP4I namespace exists, but the alert never fires even when the condition is true. What is a likely cause?
The rule is not picked up by user workload monitoring (namespace or label issues), the PromQL references a metric name or labels that do not match what is scraped, or the 'for' duration is not met
Alertmanager does not support custom rules
The cluster has too many nodes
Check that the rule is loaded, run the expression in the metrics UI to confirm it returns series, and verify the duration.
Correct: loading, query or duration issues.
The metric was named ibmmq_queue_depth, but the rule used mq_queue_depth.
Test the PromQL in the console before trusting the alert.
Which MQ-specific conditions should typically trigger alerts in production?
Queue depth approaching maximum, channels in RETRYING or STOPPED state, messages on the DLQ, the queue manager not running or failing over, and certificate expiry
Size of the MQ installation directory

For IBM MQ, the conditions that predict or indicate message-flow failure are: queue depth approaching MAXDEPTH, channels RETRYING or STOPPED, any messages arriving on the dead-letter queue, the queue manager not running or failing over, and certificates nearing expiry. Inventory-style metrics such as the number of queue definitions are not health signals.
An alert fires on any message arriving on SYSTEM.DEAD.LETTER.QUEUE in production.
DLQ depth > 0 is always worth investigating.
Messages accumulate on the dead-letter queue with reason MQRC_UNKNOWN_OBJECT_NAME (2085). What is the cause, and how should it be handled?

A sender is addressing a queue that does not exist on the receiving queue manager (for example a typo or missing definition); fix the definition or routing, then re-process the DLQ messages with a dead-letter handler (runmqdlq) using appropriate rules
The DLQ header's reason code tells why the message was dead-lettered. Fix the root cause, then replay with a DLQ handler.
Correct: missing destination; fix and replay.
Wrong: TLS failures stop the channel.
The queue ORDERS.IN was missing after a migration; once defined, runmqdlq replayed 4,312 messages.
Read the MQDLH reason code first.
A sender channel shows status RETRYING. Which diagnostic steps are MOST appropriate?

Check the queue manager error logs on both sides (AMQ messages), network reachability (host, port, DNS, firewall, route or SNI), TLS configuration match, and whether the receiver channel and listener are defined and running
RETRYING means the channel cannot start. The error logs explain why: network, TLS, definition mismatch or a remote listener down.
Correct: logs, network, TLS and definitions.
AMQ9202E remote host not available: a firewall change had blocked port 443 to the remote route.
RETRYING -> error logs on both ends.
How can ACE flow-level operational data (message counts, elapsed times, errors per flow) be collected for monitoring in CP4I?

Enable flow statistics (and accounting) in the server configuration and expose them as metrics or publications to the monitoring stack, viewing them in the ACE Dashboard or Prometheus and Grafana-style tools
ACE statistics give flow and node-level performance data, which can be exported as metrics for dashboards and alerts.
The dashboard shows errors per flow per minute and p95 node elapsed time.
Enable statistics in production at an appropriate level.
An integration runtime shows no flow metrics in Prometheus, although other runtimes do. What should be checked?
That statistics or metrics are enabled in that runtime's server configuration (serverconf) and that the ServiceMonitor selects its Service
Metrics depend on runtime configuration and scrape selection. A runtime without the right serverconf or labels will not appear.
The runtime lacked the serverconf that enables statistics; adding it restored metrics.
Compare a working runtime with the failing one.
Which API Connect subsystem stores and visualizes API call events?

The API Connect analytics subsystem receives an event record for each API call from the gateway services. Records include API, product, plan, application, consumer organization, status code and latency. It stores them (OpenSearch-based in v10) and provides dashboards and search in API Manager and the Developer Portal, with optional offload to external systems.
Wrong: stores configuration, not call analytics.
The provider sees error rates by API and consumer app in API Manager analytics.
A company must send API Connect analytics data to its enterprise SIEM or data lake. What capability supports this?
Analytics offload (for example to Kafka, syslog, HTTP or other supported targets) configured in the analytics subsystem
API Connect analytics can offload event records to external systems for long-term storage and correlation.
Analytics records are offloaded to an Event Streams topic consumed by Splunk.
Offload for SIEM, long retention or cross-system correlation.
API calls succeed, but no analytics data appears for the new gateway service. What should be checked?
That the gateway service is associated with an analytics service in Cloud Manager, and that network connectivity and certificates between gateway and analytics ingestion are valid
That the developer portal is online
Gateways send analytics to the associated analytics service. A missing association, TLS problems or blocked network paths stop ingestion.
The new regional gateway service had not been linked to the regional analytics service.
No analytics -> gateway-to-analytics association and connectivity.
Product managers want to know which consumer organizations' usage of the Gold plan is approaching its limits. Which data source is MOST suitable?
API Connect Analytics, filtered by product, plan and consumer organization or application, including rate-limit rejections (HTTP 429)
Analytics records include the API, product, plan, application and status codes, which enables business-level usage insights.
A dashboard shows the top 10 consumer orgs by calls and 429 counts for the Gold plan.
Business observability comes from API analytics.
Where can operators view Event Streams health, topic throughput and consumer group lag?
In the Event Streams UI monitoring views and through Kafka metrics exported to Prometheus (for example JMX exporter and Kafka exporter metrics) shown in dashboards
Only in the API Connect portal

Event Streams exposes health and throughput in its own UI, and can export Kafka metrics (broker JMX metrics through the Prometheus JMX exporter, plus consumer-lag metrics) to Prometheus. Those metrics feed Grafana-style dashboards and PrometheusRule alerts alongside the rest of the platform.
Grafana dashboards show bytes in and out per topic and lag per consumer group.
Enable the Kafka metrics configuration in the EventStreams CR.
One consumer group's lag stays high for only 2 of 12 partitions, while the others are near zero. What is the MOST likely cause?
Data skew (hot keys sending most records to those partitions) or slow consumers assigned to those partitions; inspect key distribution and per-partition throughput
The topic has too many partitions
The broker is out of disk
Uneven lag usually means uneven load (hot keys) or an issue with the specific consumer instance owning those partitions.
Correct: skew or a slow consumer for those partitions.
One merchant ID generated 40% of events; a composite key spread the load.
The Event Streams operator reports the EventStreams instance as 'Warning' because broker pods restarted. Which first diagnostics are appropriate?
Check the instance status conditions, broker pod events (OOMKilled, probe failures), broker logs, and resource and disk usage metrics

Diagnose top-down. The EventStreams status conditions summarize what the operator sees. Pod events then show restarts, OOMKills and probe failures. Broker logs explain the error, and resource and disk metrics confirm the underlying cause. Deleting the instance destroys evidence and data.
Events show the liveness probe failing during long GC pauses; the broker heap and limits were adjusted.
Which DataPower capabilities help troubleshoot a failing transaction in a development environment?
The multistep probe (transaction probe) to inspect each processing step and context, plus logs at an appropriate level
The probe captures the message and variables at each action, which shows where processing fails. It should be enabled only temporarily because of its overhead.
The probe showed that the map action produced an empty body because of a namespace mismatch.
The probe is powerful but heavy. Use it temporarily.
DataPower latency increases, and logs show many TLS handshakes to the same back end. What is a likely optimization?
Enable persistent connections (keep-alive) and TLS session caching for the back-end TLS client profile to avoid repeated full handshakes
Repeated full TLS handshakes are CPU and latency intensive. Connection reuse and session resumption reduce overhead.
Enabling persistent connections cut p95 latency by 60 ms.
How can DataPower metrics be collected in a CP4I environment for dashboards and alerts?
Through the DataPower metrics endpoint (Prometheus format) and status providers, scraped by Prometheus through a ServiceMonitor
Only by reading the WebGUI manually
DataPower exposes operational metrics for scraping, for example throughput, latency and resource usage.
Grafana shows DataPower transactions per second and memory per gateway pod.
Monitor gateway saturation (CPU and memory) as well as latency.
Which practice reduces alert fatigue for an integration operations team?
Alert on actionable, user-impacting conditions with clear runbook links, group related alerts, use appropriate severities and durations, and route non-urgent issues to tickets
Alert on every metric above its average
Send all alerts to everyone by email

Alert fatigue comes from noisy, unactionable alerts. Page only for actionable, user-impacting conditions. Include a runbook link and context labels, group related alerts, use severities and 'for' durations to avoid flapping, and send non-urgent issues to tickets rather than pagers.
Each alert includes a runbook URL; warnings create tickets instead of pages.
If an alert is not actionable, it should not page anyone.
Operations receive dozens of duplicate pages for one outage of an MQ queue manager, one per queue alert. What should be changed?
Configure Alertmanager grouping and inhibition rules so a 'queue manager down' alert suppresses dependent queue-level alerts, and group by service
Inhibition suppresses symptom alerts when a root-cause alert is active; grouping consolidates notifications.
An inhibit rule makes QueueManagerDown suppress QueueDepthHigh for the same qmgr label.
Root-cause alerts should inhibit symptom alerts.
Which alert design BEST detects a silent failure where an integration flow stops receiving any business events (no errors, just nothing)?

An absence or freshness alert (for example no successful messages processed for X minutes during business hours, or the oldest-message age or 'time since last event' exceeding a threshold), backed by synthetic transactions
An alert on HTTP 500 rates only
An alert when log volume increases
Silent failures produce no errors. Monitoring throughput absence, data freshness and synthetic checks catches them.
Correct: absence, freshness and synthetic monitoring.
Monitor for 'nothing happening' as well as for errors.
Which TWO elements should every production alert contain? (Select TWO.)
A clear summary of the impact and affected service or component (labels such as namespace, instance and queue)
A link to a runbook with diagnostic and remediation steps
The full message payload that triggered it

A good alert tells the responder what is affected and how badly (service, namespace, instance, queue, current value against the threshold) and links to a runbook with diagnostic and remediation steps. Alerts are widely distributed, so they must never contain message payloads, personal data or credentials.
Alert: 'Payments queue ORDERS.IN depth 8k (>5k for 10m) on qm-pay-prod. Runbook: ...'
Which command shows recent events for a pod, such as scheduling failures, image pulls and probe failures?
oc describe pod <name> (or oc get events)
Events record what happened to objects and are the first stop for scheduling, image and probe issues.
oc describe pod shows 'Back-off pulling image'.
What is the purpose of 'oc adm must-gather' with a CP4I-specific image?
Collecting diagnostic data (resources, logs, status) from the cluster and CP4I components in a structured bundle for analysis or IBM support
must-gather gathers comprehensive diagnostics. Product-specific images add CP4I data needed by support.
IBM support asks for a CP4I must-gather after an upgrade failure.
Collect must-gather before restarting things, to preserve evidence.
A CP4I instance CR shows status 'Pending' for a long time. What is the MOST effective investigation order?
Read the CR status conditions, check the operator logs for reconcile errors, then check the child resources (pods, PVCs, certificates) and their events
Delete and recreate the CR repeatedly

CP4I instances are reconciled by operators in layers: the instance CR, then the operator's reconcile loop, then child resources (pods, PVCs, Certificates, Secrets). Reading the CR status conditions, then operator logs, then the events of the child resource that is not ready finds the actual blocker, for example a Pending PVC.
Conditions mention waiting for a PVC; the PVC is Pending because no storage class is set.
Applications report intermittent MQRC 2538 (MQRC_HOST_NOT_AVAILABLE) connecting to a queue manager in OpenShift. Which areas should be investigated?
DNS resolution and route or SNI configuration, load balancer health and timeouts, the queue manager listener availability during failovers, and network policies or firewalls
2538 means the TCP connection could not be established. That points to network path, DNS or listener availability problems.
An external load balancer health check misidentified the active Native HA pod, intermittently sending traffic to replicas.
2538 = cannot reach the host or port.
An ACE flow intermittently fails with timeouts calling an HTTPS back end only from some replicas. What is a likely cause?

Inconsistent configuration or connectivity between replicas, such as a missing truststore update on some pods (old ConfigMap or Secret version not rolled out), node-specific egress or DNS issues, or a connection pool exhaustion pattern
Replica-specific failures point to differences between pods: configuration versions, nodes or network paths.
Correct: compare the failing replicas with healthy ones.
Two pods started before a truststore Secret update; a rolling restart fixed them.
Some replicas fail -> what differs between them?
A pod restarts every few minutes and 'oc describe' shows 'Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503' during heavy load. What is the likely issue?
The liveness probe is too sensitive under load (the service is slow but alive), causing unnecessary restarts; tune the probe thresholds or timeouts and address capacity
Liveness failures under load can trigger restart loops that make overload worse. Probes should detect deadlock, not slowness.
Raising timeoutSeconds from 1 to 5 and adding replicas stopped the restarts.
Liveness probe = 'is it dead?', not 'is it slow?'.
Producers receive 'TimeoutException: Topic not present in metadata after 60000 ms'. The topic exists. What should be checked?
Client connectivity to all brokers' advertised addresses, authentication and authorization (describe permission on the topic), and the exact topic name
The client cannot fetch metadata for the topic. That points to connectivity to brokers, missing describe permission or a naming mismatch.
The KafkaUser lacked Describe on the topic, so metadata calls returned no topic information.

During a major incident, end-to-end order processing slows. The gateway shows rising latency, ACE CPU is normal, MQ queue depth is rising on ORDERS.OUT, and the back-end consumer pods are throttled at their CPU limits. Where is the bottleneck, and what is the BEST immediate action?

The back-end consumers are the bottleneck (CPU throttling, rising downstream queue depth); scale out or raise limits for the consumers and verify downstream dependencies, while the gateway protects intake with rate limits
ACE is the bottleneck; add ACE replicas
The gateway is the bottleneck; add gateway replicas
MQ is the bottleneck; delete messages
Rising depth on the queue the consumers read from, plus their throttling, identifies the constrained tier. Scaling the wrong tier would not help.
Correct: identify and relieve the constrained consumers.
Wrong: the gateway latency is a symptom.
Doubling consumer replicas drained the backlog in 12 minutes.
Follow the queue: where depth grows, the slow consumer is just downstream.
Which approach is MOST effective for diagnosing an intermittent latency issue across API Connect, ACE and MQ?
Use distributed traces (or correlation IDs) to find which span dominates slow requests, then drill into that component's metrics and logs for the same time window
Read all logs from the beginning of the month

For intermittent latency across several components, distributed traces (or correlation IDs) show which span dominates the slow requests. You then drill into that component's metrics and logs for the same time window to explain why. Restarting components or raising timeouts destroys evidence and hides the problem.
Slow traces showed 90% of time spent in an MQ get-wait for replies from a slow back end.
Narrow with traces, explain with metrics and logs.
Which dashboard design BEST supports an integration operations center?
Service-oriented dashboards (per business flow: API, ACE, MQ and Kafka health with golden signals) with drill-down to component dashboards, plus business KPIs such as orders per minute
A single page listing every metric alphabetically

An operations center needs to know whether business flows are healthy. Service-oriented dashboards group the golden signals of every component in a flow (API, ACE, MQ, Kafka) with business KPIs such as orders per minute, and allow drill-down to component dashboards for diagnosis.
The 'Order to Cash' dashboard shows API calls, flow errors, queue depths and orders per minute.
Dashboards should answer 'is the business flow healthy?'.
Executives want a real-time view of business transactions (for example payments processed per minute and failure rate by channel) across CP4I. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

Emit business events or metrics from integration flows (for example ACE publishing business events to Event Streams, or business metrics exposed to Prometheus) and build business dashboards fed by them, correlated with technical health dashboards
Ask operators to count transactions manually
Derive business KPIs only from CPU usage
Business observability needs explicit business telemetry from the flows, linked to technical signals for root cause.
ACE publishes payment-completed events with channel and amount; Event Processing aggregates them into per-minute KPIs.
Technical metrics do not equal business KPIs. Instrument both.
Which MQ metrics help analyse persistent messaging performance problems?
Log write latency and log bytes written, commit rates, queue put and get rates, and CPU usage of the queue manager
Persistent throughput is bounded by log performance and commit behaviour. These metrics expose the bottleneck.
Log write latency of 8 ms explained a ceiling of about 120 commits per second per thread.
An ACE runtime shows growing memory usage over days until it is OOMKilled. What is the MOST likely cause, and how is it analysed?

A memory leak or unbounded cache in flows or custom Java code (for example static collections or large message trees held); analyse with heap dumps or ACE resource statistics, then fix the code or configure limits for caches
The CPU limit is too high
Gradual growth until OOM suggests retained objects. Heap analysis and resource statistics identify the culprit.
A JavaCompute node stored every request in a static HashMap; replacing it with a bounded cache fixed it.
Steady memory climb = leak, not load.
Before go-live, how should an architect validate that a CP4I solution meets a target of 2,000 transactions per second with p95 under 300 ms?

Run performance tests in a production-like environment (same versions, sizing, storage and network), ramp to and beyond the target with realistic payloads and mixes, measure golden signals per tier, identify bottlenecks, tune, and repeat; include failure scenarios such as a node loss under load
Test with 10 TPS and extrapolate linearly
Test only in development with mocked back ends
Realistic, production-like load tests with bottleneck analysis and failure injection are the only reliable validation.
Correct: realistic, iterative and failure-aware testing.
A test at 2,400 TPS with one worker killed shows p95 at 280 ms, which meets the target with headroom.
Test beyond the target, and test while failing.
Grafana shows a service's average latency is fine, but users complain of slowness. What metric should be examined?
Tail latency percentiles (p95 or p99), because averages hide slow outliers that users experience
Average latency over a longer window

Averages hide the experience of the slowest requests. A 120 ms average can coexist with a p99 of several seconds caused by GC pauses or a slow dependency. Track latency percentiles (p95, p99) for SLOs and alerts, because users feel the tail, not the mean.
p99 latency was 4 s despite an average of 120 ms, caused by periodic GC pauses.
Which TWO producer settings generally increase throughput at the cost of some latency? (Select TWO.)
Increasing batch.size and enabling compression (for example lz4 or zstd)
Batching and compression raise throughput by sending fewer, larger requests. acks=0 trades away durability, and the last option is invalid.
Wrong: sacrifices durability for critical data.
linger.ms=20 with zstd compression tripled throughput with a 15 ms latency cost.
What is the benefit of synthetic monitoring for API endpoints exposed through API Connect?
It proactively tests endpoints from external locations at regular intervals to detect outages and latency issues before users report them
Synthetic tests detect availability problems even when there is no real traffic, for example at night.
A synthetic check calls GET /health on the public API every minute from three regions.
No traffic does not mean healthy. Use synthetics.
A synthetic API test fails from one region but succeeds from others. What is the MOST likely area to investigate?
Region-specific networking: DNS or GSLB routing, regional gateway health, CDN or WAF rules, or firewalls for that region
Location-specific failures point to the network path or regional infrastructure, not the shared code.
The GSLB sent APAC traffic to a drained regional gateway.
Failure in one location -> path or regional component.
CP4I pods are evicted with 'The node was low on resource: memory'. Monitoring shows the node's memory is overcommitted. What should be done?
Review requests versus actual usage (pods with low requests but high usage), set realistic requests and limits (Guaranteed QoS for critical components), use quotas and LimitRanges, and add capacity
Eviction under memory pressure targets BestEffort and Burstable pods exceeding their requests. Realistic requests and enough capacity prevent it.
Setting ACE requests to observed p95 usage and adding a worker stopped the evictions.
Requests that are too low = overcommitted nodes and evictions.
Which logging approach BEST balances troubleshooting needs and data protection for integration payloads?
Log metadata (IDs, timestamps, outcome, error codes) by default; log payloads only when necessary, masked and time-boxed in controlled environments, with retention policies aligned to regulations
Always log full payloads in production
Log payloads to public cloud storage without encryption
Metadata logging supports correlation without exposing sensitive data. Payload logging should be exceptional, controlled and masked.
Correct: metadata by default, controlled payload logging.
Payment flows log transaction ID, status and duration; payload capture needs an approved change and auto-expires.
Logs are subject to data protection rules.
An API returns intermittent HTTP 503 from the gateway with 'No backend available' during deployments of the ACE runtime behind it. What is the BEST fix?
Ensure ACE rolling updates keep enough ready replicas (maxUnavailable 0, adequate replicas and PDBs, proper readiness probes) and configure gateway retry or timeout behaviour appropriately
Deployment gaps occur when all or most pods are not ready simultaneously. Rolling update strategy, readiness and replicas ensure continuous availability.
With maxUnavailable 0 and maxSurge 1, deployments no longer cause 503s.
An organization is adopting CP4I and wants an observability strategy that scales to hundreds of integrations owned by many teams. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

Define platform-wide standards (metrics naming, structured logs, correlation and trace propagation, mandatory dashboards and alerts per integration via templates), provide central collection (Prometheus or remote-write, logging, OTel collector, APM), and give teams self-service views with SLOs per business service
Let each team choose its own tools and formats with no standards
Rely on users to report incidents
Standards plus central platforms plus self-service SLO dashboards scale observability across many teams while keeping correlation possible.
Correct: standardized, centralized, self-service and SLO-driven.
A new integration template automatically includes a ServiceMonitor, a PrometheusRule, a dashboard and OTel configuration.
Observability as part of the paved road.
